**(D)** Decomposers

Counted as individuals, the decomposers (bacteria and fungi) far outnumber every other group: a single gram of soil or detritus can hold millions of bacteria. Among the grazing levels, producers are more numerous than herbivores and herbivores than carnivores, as the upright pyramid of numbers shows, but such pyramids leave out the decomposers altogether, as the chapter itself points out.

[Note: the chapter does not state this; it compares only the grazing trophic levels. Standard biology (NCERT Exemplar) gives decomposers as the group with the largest population.]

**(B)** Zooplankton

The second trophic level is made of the primary consumers (herbivores), and in a lake these are the zooplankton, which graze on phytoplankton; the chapter's chart of trophic levels names zooplankton at this level. Phytoplankton are the producers of the first trophic level, and fishes feed on zooplankton and other animals, so they sit at the third level or above. Benthos is not a trophic level but a group of organisms defined by living on the lake bottom.

**(C)** Carnivores

Secondary consumers feed on the herbivores, so they are carnivores and occupy the third trophic level, as the chapter states. Herbivores are the primary consumers, and producers are autotrophs, which make their own food by photosynthesis and so are not consumers at all.

**(B)** 50 %

The chapter states that of the total incident solar radiation, less than 50% is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), the 400 to 700 nm band that plants can use; among the options this is the matching value. The figure of 2 to 10% is a different quantity: the share of the PAR that plants actually capture. All of the incident radiation (100%) is never photosynthetically active.

**(C)** Climax community

The chapter explains that succession eventually leads to a climax community, which does not evolve further and stays stable as long as the environment remains unchanged. The intermediate communities on the way are seral communities. 'End', 'final' and 'dark' community are not ecological terms.

**(A)** Primary

A landslide strips away the vegetation together with the soil, leaving bare rock or raw subsoil where no community lived before, so colonisation has to begin with pioneers such as lichens, as on any bare rock. Secondary succession needs soil that is still present, as in abandoned farmland or a burned forest. 'Tertiary' is not a type of succession, and climax is its end stage, not a type.

[Note: the chapter does not state this; it does not mention landslides. Standard biology treats a landslide that removes the soil as a site of primary succession; where soil is left behind, succession there would be secondary.]

**(C)** Phosphorus

The chapter states that, unlike carbon and nitrogen, phosphorus is always in short supply and so acts as a limiting factor for plant growth. Its reservoir is the Earth's crust, it reaches soil and water only slowly through weathering of rock, and it has no gaseous phase to be drawn from the air. This is also why a sudden influx of phosphate from runoff causes eutrophication. Carbon and nitrogen have large atmospheric reservoirs, and sulphur is rarely the limiting nutrient.
